To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

children whose mothers are HIV infected have more behavior problems, more internalizing problems, lower levels of cognitive competence, and lower levels of prosocial competence than do children whose mothers are not HIV infected.
children of mothers who are HIV infected are at increased risk for psychosocial problems and poor academic achievement.
the children of HIV-infected mothers have higher levels of psychosocial problems than children whose mothers are not infected.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of maternal HIV infection on the development of young children.
the impact of the HIV epidemic on families and children.
the psychosocial adjustment, particularly the externalizing behavior problems and the cognitive functioning, of children whose mothers are infected with HIV.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the HIV status of mothers does not seem to be the primary determinant of children's psychosocial adjustment, and that the HIV status is only one factor in a complex web of influences that affect the lives of these families.
the psychosocial adjustment and reading achievement of children with HIV infected mothers is significantly worse than those of children with non-HIV infected mothers.
children whose mothers are HIV infected are at increased risk for a number of psychosocial problems and may be in greater need of services.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the psychosocial adjustment and cognitive development of young children whose mothers are HIV infected is significantly worse than that of children whose mothers do not report HIV infection.
children of HIV infected mothers have a higher risk of developing psychosocial problems and that this may be due, in part, to maternal depression.
children of HIV infected mothers have a greater risk for adjustment problems than children of mothers not infected with HIV.
The main takeaway from our work is that
children whose mothers are HIV infected are more likely to have problems in all domains of adjustment.
the psychosocial adjustment problems that we found in children of HIV infected mothers are not unique to this population.
the psychosocial adjustment difficulties that we found among children of mothers living with HIV were not unique to children of mothers living HIV.
